title: Ledgerline
tagline: Month-end close cut from nine days to four for a 2,400-seat payables floor.
summary: A reconciliation console that treats matching as a judgement call, not a data-entry chore.
about: Kestrel Pay processed payables for mid-market manufacturers, but its reconciliation console had been grown, not designed — eleven years of finance-team requests bolted onto one table. Close took nine days, and three of those were analysts re-checking work the system had already done. The mandate was to raise auto-match rates without hiding the machine: controllers sign their name to the close, so every automated decision had to be inspectable, reversible, and defensible to an auditor who arrives four months later.

metrics.label: Month-end close
metrics.note: Down from nine, sustained across two quarters.

metrics.label: Auto-match rate
metrics.note: Up from 62% on identical transaction volume.

metrics.label: Fewer support tickets
metrics.note: Mostly the "why did it match this?" category, now answered in-product.

metrics.label: Per exception resolved
metrics.note: From 19 clicks to 7 on the median exception path.

research.intro: Six weeks of fieldwork across four customer finance teams, deliberately timed to land on their close days rather than a quiet Tuesday.

methods.name: Contextual inquiry
methods.detail: 11 sessions observed live during month-end close, two of them at 9pm.

methods.name: Support-ticket mining
methods.detail: 2,140 tickets from 18 months, coded into 9 recurring failure shapes.

methods.name: Analytics funnel review
methods.detail: Traced 40,000 exception resolutions to find where analysts abandoned mid-task.

methods.name: Artefact analysis
methods.detail: Collected the shadow spreadsheets 7 of 11 analysts kept beside the product.

research.insight: Analysts did not distrust the matching engine. They distrusted their ability to explain it to an auditor — so they redid its work by hand to have something to point at.

painPoints.label: The silent match
painPoints.detail: Auto-matched pairs left no trace of why they matched, so analysts re-derived the logic manually before signing off.

painPoints.label: Nineteen-click exceptions
painPoints.detail: Resolving one mismatch meant four screens, two of which existed only to confirm you meant it.

painPoints.label: Shadow spreadsheets
painPoints.detail: Seven of eleven analysts kept a private tracker because the product could not show close progress by owner.

painPoints.label: Audit panic
painPoints.detail: Reconstructing a decision from four months ago took an average of 25 minutes and a Slack thread.

competitors.name: Bandelier Close
competitors.verdict: Beautiful dashboards, but every automated decision is a black box you can only accept or reject.

competitors.name: Portico ERP module
competitors.verdict: Total auditability, buried under a 1990s tree navigation nobody opens twice.

competitors.name: Netter Reconcile
competitors.verdict: Fast rules engine aimed at bookkeepers — collapses on multi-entity intercompany volume.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Nobody had made the match itself legible. Explaining a decision was treated as an audit feature bolted on later, never as the thing that lets a controller move quickly in the moment.

personas.name: Dana Okwuosa
personas.goal: Clear her queue by Thursday without leaving anything she cannot defend.
personas.frustration: Redoes work the system already did, because the system will not show its reasoning.
personas.quote: I trust it right up until someone asks me why. Then I start again from the bank file.

personas.name: Marcus Hale
personas.goal: Sign the close on time and survive the audit in April with no restatements.
personas.frustration: Cannot see whose queue is stuck until the day it makes him late.
personas.quote: I do not need it faster. I need to know at 4pm on day two whether we are going to be late.

journey.label: One month-end close, as it is actually lived

stages.name: Bank files land
stages.detail: Overnight imports drop 14,000 transactions into the queue.

stages.name: Triage the queue
stages.detail: Dana sorts by amount, not by risk, because risk is not a column.

stages.name: Re-check the auto-matches
stages.detail: Three days spent verifying decisions the engine already made correctly.

stages.name: Fight the exceptions
stages.detail: Nineteen clicks each, with two confirmation dialogs that teach nothing.

stages.name: Chase the stragglers
stages.detail: Marcus DMs four analysts to build a picture the product should have shown him.

stages.name: Sign the close
stages.detail: Nine days in, with a private spreadsheet as the real source of truth.

stages.name: April audit request
stages.detail: Reconstruct a single decision from memory, Slack, and luck.

solutions.name: Match Receipts
solutions.detail: Every automated pair carries a plain-language receipt — the rule that fired, the confidence, the two fields that clinched it — expandable inline and frozen into the audit record.

solutions.name: One-surface exceptions
solutions.detail: Exception resolution collapsed into a single split view with keyboard-first actions. Confirmation dialogs were replaced with a seven-second undo.

solutions.name: Close Board
solutions.detail: A live close view by owner, queue and risk band, so a controller can see a stall on day two instead of day eight.

solutions.name: Time-travel view
solutions.detail: Any transaction can be replayed at any past date — what the system knew, what it decided, who overrode it — in one link an auditor can be sent.

visualDesign.statement: Finance software earns trust by being boring in the right places. The language here is high-density and near-monochrome, with a single cool blue reserved exclusively for system-made decisions — so a controller scanning a screen can tell machine judgement from human judgement without reading a word. Numerals are tabular everywhere; nothing shifts as values update.

Time-travel replay of a matched pair

title: Fair Weather
tagline: First notice of loss that stops turning a bad day into a bad month.
summary: A claims intake experience built around the twenty minutes after something goes wrong.
team: Me, 1 content designer, 1 researcher, 6 engineers, 2 claims SMEs
about: Merrowfield Mutual wrote home and small-commercial property policies across storm-exposed coastal states. Their first-notice-of-loss form was a faithful digital copy of a paper document: 62 fields, ordered by how the claims system stored data rather than how a person remembers an incident. Two thirds of policyholders abandoned it and phoned instead, at a call-handling cost the business had stopped questioning. The hard part was not the form. It was that claims intake happens on the worst day of someone’s year, often outdoors, often on a cracked phone, often while a contractor waits.

metrics.label: Digital FNOL completion
metrics.note: Up from 34% — the first release moved it more than the second.

metrics.label: Intake call volume
metrics.note: Measured over the first full storm season post-launch.

metrics.label: Post-claim intake rating
metrics.note: From 3.1, on the same survey instrument.

research.intro: Research ran against real claims, not hypotheticals — including three ride-alongs with field adjusters during an active storm response.

methods.name: Diary study
methods.detail: 23 policyholders logged their first 72 hours after a loss, in their own words.

methods.name: Call-recording analysis
methods.detail: 180 intake calls transcribed and coded for the moment the caller gave up on the form.

methods.name: Field ride-alongs
methods.detail: Three days shadowing adjusters to see what intake data they actually reuse.

methods.name: Tree testing
methods.detail: Validated a loss-type taxonomy rewritten in claimant language, not policy language.

research.insight: People were not confused by the questions. They were afraid of them — every field read like a chance to say the wrong thing and lose the claim.

painPoints.label: The interrogation tone
painPoints.detail: Fields phrased in policy language read as accusatory, so claimants stalled and called a human for reassurance.

painPoints.label: All or nothing
painPoints.detail: No save state. A phone dying at field 40 meant starting over at field 1.

painPoints.label: Photos last
painPoints.detail: Image upload sat at the end, long after most people had already put the phone down.

painPoints.label: Silence after submit
painPoints.detail: A confirmation number and then nothing for four days — the single largest driver of follow-up calls.

competitors.name: Northgate Assurance
competitors.verdict: Slick mobile intake, but funnels every complex loss straight to a phone queue.

competitors.name: Halden Insurance app
competitors.verdict: Strong claim-status tracking bolted onto an intake flow that still asks for a policy number first.

competitors.name: Ravensworth Direct
competitors.verdict: Chat-led intake that feels human until it asks the same question three times.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Every competitor optimised the filing. None designed the wait. The days between submitting and hearing back were unowned territory, and that is exactly where trust was being lost.

personas.name: Rosa Villalobos
personas.goal: Get the roof tarped and understand whether she is covered before the next storm.
personas.frustration: Cannot tell which questions are required and which will be held against her.
personas.quote: I kept re-reading it. I did not want to write the wrong thing and have that be the reason they said no.

personas.name: Terrence Boyd
personas.goal: Arrive at a property already knowing what he is looking at.
personas.frustration: Half his assignments arrive with a photo of a wet ceiling and no address detail worth using.
personas.quote: Give me four good photos and the date it started. I can do the rest from the truck.

journey.label: From the moment of loss to first adjuster contact

stages.name: It happens
stages.detail: Water through the ceiling at 6am; the priority is stopping it, not filing anything.

stages.name: Stabilise
stages.detail: Buckets, towels, a call to a roofer who asks for a claim number she does not have.

stages.name: Find the policy
stages.detail: Digging for a policy number the app should never have asked her for.

stages.name: Start the form
stages.detail: Sixty-two fields in policy language, no sense of how long this will take.

stages.name: Abandon and call
stages.detail: Twelve minutes on hold to have a person confirm she is not making it worse.

stages.name: The silence
stages.detail: Four days with a confirmation number and no visible progress.

stages.name: Adjuster calls
stages.detail: Finally a human with context — the first genuinely reassuring moment.

solutions.name: Ask like a person
solutions.detail: Every question rewritten with a content designer into claimant language, with a one-line "why we ask" beneath anything that sounds legally loaded.

solutions.name: Resumable by default
solutions.detail: Intake saves on every field change and can be resumed from a text-message link — no account, no password, no re-entry.

solutions.name: Photos first
solutions.detail: Capture opens the flow while the claimant is still standing in front of the damage, with four guided shots adjusters said they actually reuse.

solutions.name: The visible wait
solutions.detail: A claim timeline showing what has happened, what is next, and who owns it — plus a named adjuster and an honest date range, not a promise.

visualDesign.statement: This one had to feel calm before it felt clever. Generous type sizes for outdoor phone use in bad light, one question per screen, and a soft violet reserved for anything the insurer commits to — dates, ownership, next steps — so a claimant scanning in a panic can find the promises. No progress percentages, which tested as pressure; a plain step count instead.

gallery.caption: Guided photo capture as the opening step
One question per screen, with "why we ask"

title: Shopfloor Signal
tagline: Gave line supervisors a downtime story they could act on before the shift ended.
summary: Downtime capture designed for gloved hands, loud rooms, and ninety free seconds.
about: Vantera ran fourteen plants on an OEE platform that produced immaculate weekly reports nobody used to change anything. Downtime reasons were logged by supervisors from memory at end of shift, which meant the data was roughly right and completely useless — everything landed in a bucket called "Other, minor stop". The mandate was to make capture fast enough to happen at the machine, in the moment, by someone wearing gloves. The constraint that shaped everything: a supervisor has about ninety uninterrupted seconds, and the room is too loud to think in.

metrics.label: OEE lift on pilot lines
metrics.note: Sustained over two quarters at three plants.

metrics.label: "Other" reason codes
metrics.note: The bucket that used to swallow a third of all downtime.

metrics.label: Median time to log a stop
metrics.note: Two taps and a reason, gloves on.

research.intro: Five days on three shop floors across two plants, including two night shifts, plus a teardown of eighteen months of reason-code data.

methods.name: Shadowing
methods.detail: 11 supervisors observed across day, swing and night shifts.

methods.name: Reason-code forensics
methods.detail: Traced 34,000 logged stops to find where the taxonomy collapsed into "Other".

methods.name: Glove testing
methods.detail: Tap-target trials with three glove types on the actual wall-mounted panels.

methods.name: Shift-handover interviews
methods.detail: What actually gets passed on verbally, and why it never reaches the system.

research.insight: Supervisors were not skipping the log because it was long. They were skipping it because it asked for a cause at the exact moment they were still fixing the effect.

painPoints.label: Cause before cure
painPoints.detail: The system demanded a root cause while the line was still down and hands were still busy.

painPoints.label: Taxonomy by committee
painPoints.detail: 84 reason codes written by corporate engineering, none in the words the floor actually uses.

painPoints.label: Gloves versus targets
painPoints.detail: Touch targets sized for a mouse, on a panel only ever used with gloves on.

painPoints.label: Reports nobody reads
painPoints.detail: Weekly PDFs arriving Monday about a problem that was solved or forgotten on Wednesday.

competitors.name: Aldergate MES
competitors.verdict: Deep scheduling engine, an interface that assumes a seated operator with a keyboard.

competitors.name: Provec OEE
competitors.verdict: Genuinely good dashboards for plant managers; nothing at all for the person at the machine.

competitors.name: Kirinmark Tablet
competitors.verdict: Right hardware instincts, wrong data model — every stop needs a cause before it can be saved.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Everyone built for the plant manager reading yesterday. Nobody built for the supervisor standing at a stopped line right now — which is the only moment the data is cheap to collect and worth anything.

personas.name: Ivan Prokopenko
personas.goal: Get the line running and hand over a shift that does not create work for the next one.
personas.frustration: Logging a stop properly costs him the same ninety seconds he needs to fix it.
personas.quote: I will tell you exactly what happened. Just not while it is still happening.

personas.name: Priya Raghunathan
personas.goal: Find the two recurring stops costing her the most, and prove it to corporate.
personas.frustration: A third of her downtime data says "Other", which is the same as no data.
personas.quote: I can defend a number. I cannot defend a bucket labelled Other.

journey.label: A single unplanned stop, from klaxon to root cause

stages.name: Line stops
stages.detail: Klaxon, andon light, and three people converging on the same machine.

stages.name: Triage
stages.detail: Ivan diagnoses by ear before he touches a panel.

stages.name: Fix
stages.detail: Eleven minutes, gloves on, both hands occupied.

stages.name: Restart
stages.detail: Line back up; the system now wants a root cause from a menu of 84.

stages.name: Defer the log
stages.detail: Tap "Other, minor stop" and promise himself he will fix it later.

stages.name: Shift handover
stages.detail: Real story told verbally to the next supervisor, recorded nowhere.

stages.name: Monday report
stages.detail: Priya reads a chart in which a third of the truth is missing.

solutions.name: Two-tap stop
solutions.detail: Logging splits in half: mark the stop in two gloved taps now, attach the cause from a phone during handover. Capture stops competing with repair.

solutions.name: Floor vocabulary
solutions.detail: 84 codes rewritten into 19, in the words supervisors used while being shadowed, with per-line ordering by actual frequency.

solutions.name: Glove-first panel
solutions.detail: Minimum 72px targets, high-contrast at a two-metre glance, and no interaction that needs precision or a second hand.

solutions.name: The shift card
solutions.detail: One card at handover: the three stops that cost this shift the most, and whether they are getting worse. It replaced the Monday PDF entirely.

visualDesign.statement: Designed to be read at two metres, in a room lit by sodium lamps, by someone who is not going to lean in. Everything is oversized, high-contrast and stripped of decoration; amber carries state and only state, so a glance across the floor tells you whether a line is fine without reading a single label. Nothing animates on the panel — motion on a shop floor means a machine is moving, and the interface has no business borrowing that signal.

gallery.caption: Line status at a two-metre glance

title: Dwell
tagline: Eleven distribution centres, 41% less driver detention, one honest appointment.
summary: Dock scheduling rebuilt around the only number carriers actually care about.
about: Northbay ran eleven distribution centres where dock appointments were booked in a portal, confirmed by email, and then ignored by everyone. Drivers waited an average of 94 minutes past their slot; carriers billed detention; site managers blamed carriers; carriers blamed sites. The mandate was to cut detention spend. The difficulty was political rather than technical — an accurate appointment makes a site look bad, so every honest signal in the system had been quietly rounded off by the people it embarrassed.

metrics.label: Driver detention hours
metrics.note: Across eleven sites, first two quarters.

metrics.label: Average dwell
metrics.note: From 94 minutes over slot down to 55.

metrics.label: Annualised detention avoided
metrics.note: Finance-validated, net of the two sites that regressed.

metrics.label: Appointments kept
metrics.note: Up from 51% — measured against the slot, not the day.

research.intro: Two weeks split between the guard shack and the yard office, plus 30 carrier dispatchers interviewed by phone because that is the only way they ever talk to anyone.

methods.name: Yard observation
methods.detail: 4 sites, 6am–2pm, counting where the 94 minutes actually went.

methods.name: Driver intercepts
methods.detail: 38 short interviews in the cab, in the queue, while waiting.

methods.name: Dispatcher interviews
methods.detail: 30 carrier-side conversations about how they really plan a route.

methods.name: Telematics reconciliation
methods.detail: Compared GPS arrival times against booked slots and logged check-ins.

research.insight: The appointment was never the problem. Every party had learned to treat it as fiction, so each one padded their own estimate — and the padding was the delay.

painPoints.label: The fiction slot
painPoints.detail: Appointment times were aspirational, so carriers padded arrivals and sites padded capacity, compounding both.

painPoints.label: Check-in by clipboard
painPoints.detail: Arrival was recorded when a guard walked out, not when the truck arrived — the gap was pure unrecorded dwell.

painPoints.label: No shared clock
painPoints.detail: Site, carrier and driver each had a different arrival timestamp, and every detention dispute became forensics.

painPoints.label: Rebooking means phoning
painPoints.detail: A delayed driver could not move a slot without a call nobody had time to take.

competitors.name: Tidewater Dock
competitors.verdict: Best-in-class booking calendar; treats what happens after the truck arrives as somebody else’s software.

competitors.name: Grantham Yard OS
competitors.verdict: Powerful yard-move orchestration for the site, nothing at all in the driver’s hand.

competitors.name: Loadway Portal
competitors.verdict: Carrier-friendly and quick to book, but the site can silently override any slot without telling anyone.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Every product served one side of the gate. None gave the site, the carrier and the driver the same timestamp — and detention disputes are, in the end, an argument about whose clock is real.

personas.name: Curtis Nwosu
personas.goal: Two more stops today, which means knowing now whether he is waiting an hour.
personas.frustration: No way to tell a late slot from a moving one until he is already parked.
personas.quote: Tell me it is going to be ninety minutes and I will go eat. Do not tell me twenty and mean ninety.

personas.name: Lorena Batiste
personas.goal: Keep doors flowing without a queue that spills onto the county road.
personas.frustration: Half her arrivals are unannounced early, and the system rewards her for looking punctual, not being punctual.
personas.quote: I can absorb a late truck. What I cannot absorb is six early ones nobody warned me about.

journey.label: One inbound load, gate to gate

stages.name: Book the slot
stages.detail: Dispatcher picks a time everyone privately treats as approximate.

stages.name: Roll in
stages.detail: Curtis pads by 45 minutes because being late is worse than waiting.

stages.name: Arrive early
stages.detail: Parks on the shoulder; nothing in the system knows he is there.

stages.name: Check in
stages.detail: Clipboard at the shack, timestamp written when the guard gets to him.

stages.name: Wait
stages.detail: Ninety-four minutes with no visibility and no way to leave.

stages.name: Door assignment
stages.detail: A yard hostler waves him in; no notice, no ETA before it happens.

stages.name: Unload and out
stages.detail: Fast once it starts — the dock was never the bottleneck.

stages.name: Detention dispute
stages.detail: Three weeks later, two clocks disagree and someone eats the cost.

solutions.name: The honest slot
solutions.detail: Appointments show a live confidence band instead of a single time, recalculated from real door throughput. Sites stopped being punished for accuracy, so accuracy appeared.

solutions.name: Geofence check-in
solutions.detail: Arrival is stamped when the truck crosses the geofence, not when a guard notices. The clipboard became a fallback rather than the system of record.

solutions.name: One clock, three views
solutions.detail: Driver, site and carrier read the same timeline off the same events — the detention conversation moved from forensics to arithmetic.

solutions.name: Self-serve reslot
solutions.detail: A running-late driver can shift their own slot from a text link if capacity allows, and the site sees it before the truck does.

visualDesign.statement: Three audiences, one system, wildly different conditions — a phone in bright sun with one thumb, a yard-office monitor, a dispatcher’s third browser tab. The language leans on a single green used only for confirmed, shared facts; anything estimated stays outlined and uncoloured. That one rule does most of the work: on any screen, filled means agreed, and agreed is the only thing anyone can bill against.
